name: Lemon Rice
cuisine: South Indian (Karnataka chitranna / Tamil elumichai sadam)

ingredients.name: Sona masuri rice (or any short/medium-grain white rice; basmati also works), raw
ingredients.householdMeasure: ⅓ cup + 1 tbsp raw / about 1½ cups cooked

ingredients.name: Water (for cooking the rice, skip if using leftover rice)
Groundnut oil (peanut oil; sesame/gingelly oil or coconut oil also traditional)
Peanuts (moongphali), raw, with or without skin

equipment: Small kadai, tadka pan or frying pan (about 7–8 inch)
Saucepan with lid, pressure cooker or rice cooker (only if cooking the rice fresh)
Large plate or steel thali, for spreading the rice to cool
Lemon squeezer, or a fork and a small strainer to catch the seeds
Measuring spoons (normal teaspoons are a fine stand-in)
Small plate for the roasted peanuts

steps.title: Cook the rice (skip if using leftover rice)
steps.text: Rinse 75 g raw rice 2–3 times until the water runs almost clear. Cook it with 170 ml water: in a covered saucepan on low heat for 15–18 min, or a pressure cooker for 2 whistles on medium.
steps.tip: Use slightly less water than for eating plain rice so the grains stay firm. No measuring? Boil the rice in a big pot of water for 12–14 min and drain it.
steps.visualCue: All water absorbed; grains are soft but each holds its shape. A grain pressed between your fingers squashes fully with no hard centre.
steps.cameraCheck: The cooked rice in the pan, lid off
steps.videoShot: The lid lifting off to show fluffy, steaming rice.
steps.watchOut: Too much water or overcooking gives soft, pasty rice that turns to mush later. If the grains look split and sticky, use it for curd rice instead and cook a fresh, firmer batch.

steps.title: Spread the rice out to cool
steps.text: Tip the cooked rice onto a large plate and spread it into a thin layer with the spatula. Leave it to cool.
steps.tip: This is the most important step for texture. Cooled rice gives separate, fluffy grains.
steps.visualCue: No steam rises; the rice feels just warm or at room temperature, and the grains look separate.
steps.cameraCheck: The rice spread in a thin layer on the plate
steps.videoShot: The spatula spreading the rice across a steel plate.
steps.watchOut: Mixing while the rice is still hot and steaming, which makes it clump and turn sticky. If steam still rises, give it 5 more minutes or fan it with a plate.

steps.title: Squeeze the lemon
steps.text: Cut a lemon in half and squeeze one half through a strainer into a small bowl. You need 1 tbsp (15 ml) juice.
steps.tip: Roll the lemon firmly on the counter before cutting it; it gives more juice. Use fresh lemon, not bottled.
steps.visualCue: Clear pale-yellow juice with no seeds.
steps.cameraCheck: 1 tbsp lemon juice in a bowl or spoon
steps.videoShot: The lemon being squeezed over a strainer.
steps.watchOut: Seeds or pith in the juice, which make the rice bitter. If you see any seed in the bowl, lift it out with a spoon.

steps.title: Chop the chilli and ginger
steps.text: Slit or finely chop ½–1 green chilli (3 g). Peel and finely chop ½ tsp ginger (3 g). Break the dried red chilli in two.
steps.visualCue: Small, even pieces you can barely see once mixed in.
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped chilli, ginger and broken red chilli on the board
steps.videoShot: The knife chopping the ginger finely.
steps.watchOut: Large chunks of ginger or chilli, which give one very hot or sharp bite. If a piece is bigger than a rice grain, chop it again.

steps.title: Set out the tempering
steps.text: Put the mustard seeds (¼ tsp), chana dal (1 tsp) and urad dal (½ tsp) together in a small bowl. Keep the curry leaves, hing and turmeric next to the stove.
steps.tip: Having everything ready stops the dals burning while you hunt for the next item.
steps.cameraCheck: The small bowl of mustard seeds and dals, with curry leaves beside it
steps.videoShot: Overhead shot of the small bowls lined up near the stove.
steps.watchOut: Starting the oil before everything is ready. The tempering takes under 3 minutes, so if you are still measuring when the oil is hot, switch off the flame while you finish.

steps.title: Heat the oil
steps.text: Put the kadai on medium heat and add 2 tsp (10 ml) oil.
steps.visualCue: The oil shimmers and flows thinly when you tilt the pan, and a mustard seed dropped in sizzles at once.
steps.watchOut: Oil that smokes. Smoking oil tastes bitter; if it smokes, take the pan off the heat for 30 seconds and lower the flame.

steps.title: Roast the peanuts
steps.text: Add 1 heaped tbsp (12 g) peanuts. Stir often on medium-low heat until crunchy, then lift them out onto a small plate, leaving the oil in the pan.
steps.tip: Taking the peanuts out keeps them crunchy. Bite one: it should snap, not feel soft or raw.
steps.visualCue: The peanuts turn golden-brown, the skins (if on) darken and crack, and they smell nutty.
steps.cameraCheck: The roasted peanuts on the plate
steps.videoShot: Peanuts tossing in the oil and changing colour.
steps.watchOut: Peanuts that look pale and soft (undercooked) or go dark brown quickly (burnt, bitter). They keep cooking on the plate, so lift them out when they are light golden.

steps.title: Crackle the mustard seeds
steps.text: With the heat at medium, add the mustard seeds, chana dal and urad dal from the bowl.
steps.tip: Keep a lid handy; the seeds can spit.
steps.visualCue: The mustard seeds pop and crackle within about 10 seconds.
steps.cameraCheck: The seeds and dals in the oil
steps.videoShot: Mustard seeds jumping and popping in the oil.
steps.watchOut: Seeds that do not pop (oil not hot enough, giving a raw taste) or that fly out of the pan. If nothing pops after 20 seconds, raise the heat slightly; if they spit, cover the pan loosely.

steps.title: Fry the dals golden
steps.visualCue: The chana dal and urad dal turn light golden (not brown) and smell toasty.
steps.cameraCheck: The golden dals in the kadai
steps.videoShot: Close-up of the dals turning from pale to golden.
steps.watchOut: Dal turning dark brown, which tastes bitter and spoils the dish. Turn the heat down as soon as it colours; if it goes dark brown, start the tempering again.

steps.title: Add the chillies, ginger and curry leaves
steps.text: Add the red chilli, green chilli, ginger and curry leaves. Stir.
steps.tip: Stand slightly back; wet leaves pop.
steps.visualCue: The curry leaves turn crisp and bright, and the ginger smells sharp and fragrant.
steps.cameraCheck: The tempering with curry leaves in the pan
steps.videoShot: Curry leaves hitting the oil and spluttering.
steps.watchOut: Wet curry leaves that splatter hard, and ginger that browns and turns bitter. Pat the leaves dry beforehand and move to the next step as soon as the leaves stop spluttering.

steps.title: Add the hing and turmeric
steps.text: Lower the heat. Add a small pinch of hing and ⅛ tsp turmeric. Stir.
steps.visualCue: The oil turns bright yellow and the hing smell blooms.
steps.cameraCheck: The yellow tempering in the pan
steps.videoShot: The turmeric dusting in and the oil turning yellow.
steps.watchOut: Turmeric burning in seconds, which turns the oil brown and bitter. Move straight to the next step; if it darkens, the tempering cannot be rescued, so start again.

steps.title: Add the rice and salt
steps.text: Turn the heat to low. Add the cooled rice (about 225 g) and ¼ tsp salt.
steps.visualCue: A mound of white rice on top of the yellow tempering.
steps.cameraCheck: The rice in the kadai, before mixing
steps.videoShot: The rice being tipped into the kadai.
steps.watchOut: Dropping the rice in as one big lump, which then needs hard mixing and breaks the grains. Crumble any lumps with your fingers as it goes in.

steps.title: Mix gently
steps.text: Fold the rice over the tempering with a flat spatula, lifting from underneath, until every grain is evenly yellow. Warm it through for 1–2 min on low.
steps.visualCue: Evenly yellow rice with grains still separate, flecked with dals and curry leaves. It is warm, not sizzling.
steps.videoShot: The spatula folding the rice in slow scoops.
steps.watchOut: Hard stirring, which breaks the grains into a paste, and white patches where the tempering has not reached. Fold in slow scoops; fridge rice may need 1 extra minute to warm through.

steps.title: Add the lemon juice off the heat
steps.text: Switch off the flame. Pour the 1 tbsp lemon juice over the rice and fold it in.
steps.visualCue: The rice looks slightly glossy and smells fresh and tangy.
steps.cameraCheck: The lemon juice going over the rice
steps.videoShot: Lemon juice drizzling over the yellow rice.
steps.watchOut: Adding lemon juice while the pan is still on the flame, which can turn it bitter and dull the colour. Always switch off first; if the rice tastes bitter later, balance it with a pinch of salt.

steps.title: Add the peanuts and taste
steps.text: Fold in the roasted peanuts (keep a few for the top) and the coriander leaves. Taste a spoonful and add a pinch more salt or a few more drops of lemon if needed.
steps.cameraCheck: A spoonful of finished lemon rice
steps.videoShot: The peanuts going in and a spoon lifting some rice.
steps.watchOut: Too little salt or lemon, which makes the rice taste flat. Add a pinch of salt or a few drops of lemon a little at a time and taste again.

steps.title: Rest, then serve
steps.text: Cover and leave it for 5 minutes so the rice absorbs the lemon and tempering. Serve topped with the remaining peanuts.
steps.tip: Many South Indian cooks say lemon rice tastes even better an hour later, which is why it is a classic lunchbox and travel dish.
steps.visualCue: Bright yellow, fluffy rice with crunchy peanuts on top; it smells of lemon, curry leaves and roasted dal.
steps.videoShot: The lid lifting off, then the rice spooned onto a plate.
steps.watchOut: Serving straight away, when the lemon taste sits only on the surface, or leaving it open so the rice dries out. Keep it covered for the full 5 minutes.

reasons: a light, plant-based meal with only 2 tsp oil, no deep frying and no cream. Peanuts and the two dals add some protein, healthy fats and crunch, and turmeric, curry leaves and lemon add flavour without calories. Points come off because it is mostly white rice (high glycaemic load, low fibre) and protein is modest at about 11 g for 470 kcal; sodium is about 30% of the daily limit. Restaurant versions tend to use more oil or ghee, cashews, more salt and bigger rice portions, and are often eaten alone without a vegetable or protein side.

researchRating.basis: lemon rice (chitranna) is one of South India's best-loved everyday rice dishes, a staple of lunchboxes, temple prasadam and travel food. Recipe sites rate it very highly: Swasthi's Recipes about 4.99/5 from roughly 290–300 votes, Hebbar's Kitchen 5/5 from 187 votes, Cup of Yum 4.9 from 156 reviews, Tarla Dalal 4.9/5 from 12 reviews, Slurrp 4.2 from 13 ratings and Whisk Affair 5 from 3 votes. Small deduction because it is seen as a simple, everyday dish rather than a showpiece, recipe-site ratings skew high, and several samples are small.

storage: Refrigerate in an airtight box within 1–2 hours of cooking (cooked rice should not sit out longer, because of Bacillus cereus risk). It keeps for 1–2 days in the fridge. Freezing works for up to 1 month, but the peanuts soften; add fresh roasted peanuts after reheating. To reheat, sprinkle 1–2 tsp water and microwave covered for 1–1½ min, stirring once, or warm in a pan on low heat with a lid for 2–3 min until steaming hot all through. Reheat only once.
leftoverRemix: Lemon rice tikki (crispy rice cutlets). Mash 1 cup leftover lemon rice with 1 small boiled potato, 2 tbsp besan and 1 tbsp chopped onion. Shape into 4 small patties and shallow-fry in 1 tsp oil on a tawa for 3 min per side until golden. Serve with green chutney or ketchup as a tea-time snack.
burnOff: about 6.7 km of running (470 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 9.4 km of brisk walking (about 1 hr 50 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.).

navratri.reason: rice, chana dal, urad dal, mustard seeds and hing are not allowed under the common vrat rule set (assumed; families differ)

ekadashi.reason: rice and dals are commonly avoided on Ekadashi (common rule set assumed; families differ)

jain.reason: swap the fresh ginger for a pinch of sonth; no onion, garlic or potato in the recipe

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; light and quick, though mostly white rice with modest protein (about 600 mg sodium)

jain.reason: drop the fresh ginger (3 g, a root); use a pinch of dry ginger powder (sonth) instead; hing is allowed (see Jain variant)

vegan.reason: no dairy, ghee, honey or egg (made with groundnut oil)

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian recipe with no meat, fish or egg

sattvik.reason: the recipe has no onion or garlic

glutenFree.reason: most hing (asafoetida) sold in India is compounded with wheat flour; use a hing labelled gluten-free or leave it out (see Gluten-free variant)

dairyFree.reason: no curd, ghee or milk in the recipe (the optional ghee finish is left out)

variants.reason: main recipe already vegan (groundnut oil, no dairy or egg)
